## Abstract

Nitrogen-doped graphene (N-G) catalyst emerges as one of promising non-platinum group

metal (non-PGM) catalysts with the advantages of low cost, high oxygen reduction reaction

(ORR) activity, stability, and selectivity to replace expensive PGM catalysts in electrochemical

systems. In this research, nanoscale high energy wet (NHEW) ball milling is first investigated for

the synthesis of N-G catalysts to make conventional problems such as sintering or localized

overheating issues negligible. The successful synthesis of N-G catalysts with comparable

catalytic performance to 10 wt% Pt/C by using this method has been published. This paper

focuses on understanding the effect of grinding speed and grinding time on the particle size and

chemical state of N-G catalysts through the physical and chemical characterization. The research

result shows that 1) the final particle size, nitrogen doping percentage, and nitrogen bonding

composition of synthesized N-G catalysts are predictable and controllable by adjusting the

grinding time, the grinding speed, and other relative experimental parameters; 2) the final

particle size of N-G catalysts could be estimated from the derived relation between the cracking

energy density and the particle size of ground material in the NHEW ball milling process with

specified experimental parameters; 3) the chemical composition of N-G catalysts synthesized by

NHEW ball milling is controllable by adjusting the grinding time and grinding speed.

## 1. Introduction

There have been intense researches being performed on “synthesis” and “catalysis” of

catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in electrochemical systems in the past decades

[1, 2]. So far, the most effective electrocatalyst for ORRs is platinum (Pt) and its alloys in the

form of nanoparticles dispersed on carbon black supports, usually Vulcan carbon, which

proceeds through a four-electron transfer mechanism [3, 4]. Platinum provides the lowest

overpotential and the highest selectivity toward the direct oxygen reduction to water, yielding

only a small amount of hydrogen peroxide. However, the high cost, limited supply, and poor

durability and stability of platinum have hindered the large-scale application of ORR

electrochemical systems [4]. To reduce the amount of platinum required for applications, a range

of non-PGM catalysts exhibiting good activity for the ORR has been reported.

Currently, there is a tremendous research work being made in the fields of non-PGM

catalysts [5]. The non-PGM catalysts are intended to be synthesized with nonmetallic substances

and metals but without any precious metal element. Significant progress in non-PGM catalysts

has emerged with the advent of new carbon structures such as carbon nanowires, nanotubes, and

graphenes doped with nitrogen [6]. Recently, it has been demonstrated that the nitrogen-doped

graphene (N-G) catalyst shows an outstanding ORR catalytic activity which is comparable to Pt

catalysts for ORR [7]. The N-G catalyst has shown a potential as the ORR catalyst of low cost,

high stability, and high efficiency. In spite of extensive studies, the exact catalytic mechanism of

N-G is still under debate. A fundamental disagreement lies in how nitrogen contributes to the

catalysis. The key to answering this question is to determine the contribution of four nitrogen

doping configurations, namely pyridinic nitrogen, graphitic nitrogen, pyrrolic nitrogen, and

pyridine-N-oxide (or pyridine N+-O-, or pyridine +N-O-), to the catalytic performance [8]. The

key influencing factors of the chemical state of synthesized N-G catalysts are the synthesis

approach and experimental conditions.

It is well known that chemical methods, such as chemical vapor deposition (CVD), thermal

treatment, or plasma treatment, are effective on the synthesis of N-G catalysts [9]. But the

challenges such as overheating, sintering, coking, or high-temperature safety issues will exist

during the integration process [8]. These problems can be solved if N-G catalysts can be

synthesized at a normal temperature or room temperature. Recent studies of the ball milling

ball milling, which is generally used for industrial grinding, is a type of mechanochemical

on the research of ball milling, a new nanoscale high energy wet (NHEW) ball milling is first

introduced as a primary synthesis approach for N-G catalysts in conjunction with the research

work previously published [13]. A water reaction environment was applied to the environment of

the reaction between graphene oxide (GO) and melamine for the synthesis of N-G catalysts. The

purpose of using deionized water as the reaction environment is to well disperse GO and

melamine to increase the amount of doped nitrogen in N-G catalysts, reduce the wear rate of the

reactor and grinding media, and enhance the grinding efficiency. Several N-G catalysts were

generated by NHEW ball milling and characterized in the research work previously published

[13]. The problems from sintering, overheating and high-temperature safety issues were not

observed during the synthesis process. The characterization results confirm that N-G catalysts

were efficiently synthesized under room temperature and water environment with NHEW ball

milling approach. The ORR test result from rotating ring disk electrode (RRDE) method in

## 2. Experimental Methodology

### 2.1. Synthesis Section

N-G catalysts were synthesized by the NHEW ball milling method in the synthesis section.

The synthesis reaction mechanism and synthesis processing control were studied through the

characterization of physical and chemical properties of synthesized N-G catalysts under electron

microscopy and electron spectroscopy.

The N-G catalysts were synthesized by grinding GO and melamine powders under deionized

water environment in a planetary ball milling machine (PM100, Retsch Inc.). The reaction

mechanism is that the mechanical energy, which is generated by the milling process, activates

reactants and makes the synthesis reaction occur during the grinding process. The solid particles

are destroyed to small particles and activated by collision from the grinding media. Therefore,

nitrogen atoms from melamine can be doped on activated GO particles to form N-G catalysts at

the temperature much lower than the temperature required for using conventional chemical

methods. The whole process is performed at room temperature. The final temperature of the

ground material after NHEW ball milling was 28℃ at 200 RPM/24 hours condition, and 67℃ at

650 RPM/24 hours condition. Therefore, the problem such as sintering, overheating or coking

was negligible during the synthesis process. It is well known that the grinding speed and grinding

time are primary influencing factors during the ball milling process [14]. The synthesis process

can be controlled by adjusting grinding speed and grinding time with the same grinding jar and

grinding media conditions.

*Figure 2 shows the process of synthesizing N-G catalysts by NHEW ball milling approach.*

The primary synthesis process is as follows: First, GO particles as a carbon source, and

melamine particles as a nitrogen source are mixed in the deionized water (8 mL) with a specific

weight ratio (GO: melamine = 1:6, GO= 5 mg). The suspension solution is heated (to 60 °C) to

dissolve melamine in the solution. The solution is cooled to room temperature (22 °C) and

dispersed by an ultrasonic cleaner (power: 75 W) to produce a well-dispersed precursor solution.

The precursor solution (8 mL) is then moved to a stainless steel grinding jar (12 mL, inner

diameter=30 mm) with grinding balls (1.4–1.7-mm diameter, volume = 6mL) made of zirconia.

The materials are ground at a specific grinding speed for a particular grinding time to prepare N-

G catalyst samples. The ground solution is water bath heated to 60℃ and then centrifuged to

remove unreacted melamine particles and soluble components. The solid powders are dried in a

vacuum oven after thrice centrifugation, and the final product remains as N-G catalysts.

*Figure 2. Schematic representation of the NHEW ball milling process. Nitrogen atoms from melamine are doped on GO particles and formed special N-functional groups with ORR catalytic activity.*

The chemical structural formula shows that the N=C bonding and –NH2 bonding in

melamine particles can provide nitrogen atoms for the nitrogen doping process. At the first stage

of the doping process, the nitrogen ions are released from the decomposed melamine particles by

ball milling. Meanwhile, GO particles are broken into smaller pieces and activated by ball

milling. Then the nitrogen ions are adsorbed on the active surfaces of GO and formed new

chemical bonds with activated carbon atoms. The activation energy of the reaction is from ball

milling as well. All the products generated by doping nitrogen on GO are nitrogen-doped

graphene structural materials. But only the nitrogen-doped graphene, which has particular

nitrogen functional groups such as pyrrolic-N, pyridnic-N, graphitic-N, and pyridine-N-oxide,

can be considered as the ORR N-G catalyst.

This paper shows the results on 1) the controllable synthesis of N-G catalysts, 2) electron

microscope imaging of the microstructure of N-G catalysts, and 3) X-ray spectroscopy analysis

of the chemical composition and the local structure of N-G catalysts. The characterization result

will give great insights on the investigation of the controllability of the synthesis by

understanding the influences of experimental conditions on the physical structure, chemical

composition, the ORR activity and selectivity of N-G catalysts synthesized by NHEW ball

milling.

### 2.2. Characterization Section

The synthesized N-G catalysts are characterized by several characterization approaches

include the Zetasizer, Scanning electron microscope (SEM), Transmission electron microscopy

(TEM), the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), X-ray diffraction (XRD) and Fourier

## 3. Result and Discussion

### 3.1 Experimental Parameters

Several experimental conditions can influence the synthesis results in the NHEW ball milling

process, include grinding time, grinding speed, the type of the mill machine, material of the

milling media, and the ratio between milling media, two reactants, and water. But three initial

conditions, which are grinding time, grinding speed, and the ratio between reactants,

significantly influence the physical and chemical properties of the final product. Most of the

influencing factors were invariable in this experiment, exclude grinding speed and grinding time.

The effects of grinding time and grinding speed on characteristics of N-G products were

investigated in this research to understand the synthesis reaction mechanism of N-G by NHEW

ball milling and realize the controllability of the final product. A series of N-G catalysts

generated at different grinding time step were characterized to investigate the changes of GO by

doping nitrogen during ball milling and the effect of the grinding time increment on the synthesis

of N-G catalysts. Another series of N-G catalysts synthesized with same experimental parameters

but different grinding speeds were characterized to understand the effect of the grinding speed on

the synthesis of N-G catalysts.

### 3.2. Characterization of the Microstructure of N-G Catalysts

A successful ball milling can be directly confirmed through the breakage of particles and the

structural modification. It is already proved that the dry ball milling can easily break bulk solid

powders to small particles. But the high wear rate of the grinding media and grinding jar leads to

the additional material cost and low purity of the final product. The impurities may have an

adverse impact on the electrochemical performance of N-G catalysts. Therefore, NHEW ball

milling is designed to synthesize N-G in this research. The water environment in the grinding jar

can reduce the wear rate and noise. But the movement of the grinding media and the grinding

energy can be affected by water as well. It was unknown that if the GO 2D sheet could be

fractured during the wet ball milling process. The structural changes of precursor and nitrogen-

doped graphene materials during the NHEW ball milling process were investigated in this

research to confirm the fracture of ground materials and understand the reaction mechanism of

the synthesis of N-G catalysts.

The structural changes of N-G samples in Series 1 and Series 2 were investigated through

Zetasizer, SEM and TEM observation in this research. The N-G catalyst synthesized by NHEW

ball milling method relies on the complex chemical reactions, and thus it is essential to identify

the micro/nanostructures of the final product to confirm the fidelity of the proposed reaction

routes. The particle size distributions of N-G catalysts were characterized by Zetasizer, which

has high accuracy on the measurement of the particle size from 10 nm to 10 μm. The

nanostructural properties of N-G catalysts were characterized by SEM and TEM imaging. The

surface structure of N-G samples in the Series 1 and Series 2 were evaluated by SEM imaging.

3.2.1.1. Zetasizer result of Series 1 samples

The measured final particle sizes of the N-G samples in Series 1 are shown in Figure 5 and

*Table 3. The particle size in this figure is the peak value in the particle size distribution of a*

The particle size of BM-N-G-32-500 is down to 310.8 nm from the initial average particle size of

supplier (Graphene Supermarket). This result shows that the particles from the GO precursor

were decomposing during wet ball milling process. Therefore, the particle size of the N-G

catalyst can be reduced from 5 μm to 310.8 nm by NHEW ball milling with the specific

experimental conditions. But the relation between the particle size and the grinding time is not

3.2.1.3. Discussion of the collision model

The analysis of the Zetasizer results of samples in Series 1 and Series 2 shows that the

grinding time and grinding speed are two of influencing factors on the final particle size of

ground N-G materials. It is known that grinding time and grinding speed are directly related to

the mechanical energy generated by the planetary ball milling. In other words, the energy

transferred from the mill to the ground materials is the primary factor on the final particle size of

N-G catalysts. In this experiment, collisions between grinding balls, ground materials and the

wall of the jar are assumed to be the primary mechanism by which energy is transferred from the

mill to the ground materials during the wet ball milling process. Therefore, the main parameters

of the collision model of the wet-planetary ball milling process to evaluate are the kinetic energy

of the grinding balls, the energy transfer percentage of the kinetic energy of the materials in a

collision, and the amount of ground materials in a collision.

## 4. Conclusion

The N-G catalyst with high ORR catalytic performance is firstly synthesized by the NHEW

ball milling method in this research [30-32]. The research shows a possibility to synthesize N-G

catalysts at room temperature condition by the mechanochemical approach. The changes of the

GO/Melamine precursor during the synthesis process were investigated through the physical and

chemical characterization of a series of N-G samples selected from one N-G synthesis process.

Another investigation of this research is the processing control of synthesizing N-G by NHEW

ball milling method. The physical and chemical characterization results show that the process of

doping nitrogen on GO by NHEW ball milling is a time-related and grinding speed-related

process. It is possible to control the properties of the final product through the setting of grinding

speed and grinding time. The detailed conclusions are following:

(1) The decomposition of the GO/Melamine precursor in the NHEW ball milling process is

influenced by several experimental conditions include the grinding time and grinding speed. The

final particle size of N-G catalysts could be derived from the relation equation of the cracking

energy density to the particle size. The experimental data shows that it is possible to control the

final particle size and the decomposition rate of ground materials by adjusting the grinding time,

the grinding speed, and other relative experimental parameters.

(2) The nitrogen doping process is a time & grinding speed-related process. The nitrogen

content of the N-G catalysts was increasing during 32 hours NHEW ball milling. Meanwhile, the

nitrogen content of N-G catalysts increased with the increasing grinding speed. The reason is the

growing amount of new active sites on the GO particles available for doping nitrogen.

(3) It is observed from FTIR and XPS results that the atomic percentage of the N-C bond

increased with the decreasing atomic proportion of the C-O bond. And the nitrogen content

increased with the decreasing oxygen content during 32 hours grinding process. The formation

curves of pyrrolic-N, pyridinic-N, graphitic-N and pyridine-N-oxide during 32 hours wet ball

milling show that the highest formation rate of pyrrolic-N and pyridinic-N bonds is located at the

first 8 hours grinding stage, where the highest decomposition rate of the GO/Melamine precursor

is found. Otherwise, the formation rate of graphitic-N and pyridine-N-oxide is increasing during

32 hours grinding process.

(4) The relative percentages of pyridinic-N, graphitic-N, and pyridine-N-oxide in the

nitrogen bonding composition of N-G catalysts were increasing with the increasing grinding


<!-- Page 27 -->


25

speed during 16 hours grinding process. The previous research shows that the relative ratio

between pyrrolic-N, pyridinic-N, graphitic-N and pyridine-N-oxide has a significant effect on the

ORR catalytic activity and selectivity of N-G catalysts. Meanwhile, the nitrogen bonding

composition of N-G catalysts at different time stage of 32 hours grinding process in analyzed. On

the other hand, the particle size of the final N-G product synthesized with 16 hours grinding time

and specified grinding speed (not higher than 500 RPM) is predictable from an estimation

equation. Therefore, it is possible to control the particle size, the nitrogen content, and the

relative ratio between four particular nitrogen bonds in N-G catalysts, by adjusting the

experimental setting of grinding time and grinding speed.
